title: EPA Dismantles Key Biden-Era Climate Rule
text:
(Thinkstock via Getty Images)

The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) repealed greenhouse gas regulations for coal- and natural gas-fired power plants Monday, setting up another likely legal fight over the federal government’s authority to regulate the power sector under the Clean Air Act.

The rollback would eliminate more than $300 billion in costs for the energy industry and allow utilities to make decisions based on the needs of their ratepayers rather than potentially shuttering aging power plants, according to the EPA. The repeal reverses Biden-era regulations requiring existing coal plants and certain new natural gas plants to capture 90% of their carbon emissions by 2032 if they planned to continue operating past 2039. (RELATED: Democrats Go Quiet On Climate After Biden-Era Regulatory Blitz)

“America should be producing more affordable, reliable energy, not forcing power plants and taxpayers to spend billions capturing and burying CO₂,” Jason Isaac, founder and CEO of the American Energy Institute, told the Daily Caller News Foundation.

TODAY: EPA is set to eliminate needless CO₂ regulations that pushed power plants toward costly carbon capture, raising rates for Americans.TOMORROW: The @txrrc is set to approve a massive carbon capture project positioned to collect billions in Biden-era Green New Scam tax…

“Administrator Zeldin is right to reject regulations designed to constrain the energy Americans depend on and to restore the Clean Air Act to its proper purpose,” Isaac said.

The EPA first proposed repealing the power plant greenhouse gas standards on June 11, 2025, arguing at the time that eliminating the regulations would reduce costs and bolster grid reliability.

“Repealing the power plant rule for greenhouse gas emissions is key to the Trump energy agenda,” Steve Milloy, senior legal fellow at the Energy & Environment Legal Institute and former Trump EPA transition team member, told DCNF. “Now, it will have to be defended in court.”

“Concurrently with the Trump EPA’s final rule, we are proposing to rescind all remaining greenhouse gas emissions (GHG) requirements for power plants, which have imposed unnecessary requirements and drained the power sector’s resources, while producing virtually no benefit,” the EPA press office told DCNF.

The legal fight over how the EPA can regulate power plant emissions stretches back to West Virginia and other states petitioning the Supreme Court in 2021 after the D.C. Circuit struck down the Trump administration’s Affordable Clean Energy rule and its repeal of the Obama-era Clean Power Plan, according to the Supreme Court docket in West Virginia v. EPA.

“[I]t’s the Biden administration that failed to account for the U.S. Supreme Court decision in West Virginia v. EPA. That historic decision barred EPA from misusing the Clean Air Act (CAA) to manipulate Americans’ energy choices,” the EPA said.

The Supreme Court ruled 6-3 against the EPA in June 2022 in an opinion led by Chief Justice John Roberts.

“The manipulation in the 2024 Biden rule created inefficient uses of natural gas, adversely impacted the nation’s energy systems, and drove electricity prices up,” EPA press office said. “The 2024 rule was another example of the Democrats’ war on America’s natural resources and attempted to achieve the same unlawful fuel-shifting goals of the Obama-era Clean Power Plan.”

The Court determined that the Clean Air Act did not give the EPA the authority to impose the Obama administration’s generation-shifting approach, which sought to move electricity production away from higher-emitting sources such as coal toward lower-emitting sources.

The Court applied the major questions doctrine, reasoning that an agency claiming authority over an issue of major economic and political significance needs clear authorization from Congress, according to the Court’s opinion.

The decision did not categorically prohibit the EPA from regulating greenhouse gas emissions from power plants. The Biden administration subsequently issued a different set of regulations in April 2024 governing greenhouse gas emissions from new and existing fossil fuel-fired power plants, according to the EPA.

Those standards relied in part on carbon capture and sequestration to establish emissions requirements for certain coal-fired plants and new natural gas facilities.

“Models continue to show that GHG emissions from power plants have no material impact on global climate change. In fact, if all carbon dioxides were eliminated tomorrow, there would be no meaningful climate impact,” the EPA told the DCNF.

“Challengers will almost certainly take aim at EPA’s claim that U.S. power plants are not significant contributors to global carbon dioxide levels and therefore future temperatures,” Isaac Orr, vice president of research at Always On Energy Research, told the DCNF.

Lawsuits from environmental organizations, including the Natural Resources Defense Council (NRDC) and Sierra Club challenging the rollback, are to be expected, Orr said.

The NRDC said the EPA’s action is based on flawed legal and technical analysis and “will not survive legal challenge.”

NRDC, the Sierra Club, Environmental Defense Fund, Earthjustice and other environmental groups have also brought legal challenges against other recent EPA climate rollbacks, according to Earthjustice.

“Following the repeal of the 2009 Endangerment Finding, and the U.S. Supreme Court decision in Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo, EPA’s proposal states that CAA Section 111 does not give the agency the authority to regulate power plant emissions based on climate change,” according to the EPA.

The power plant action follows the administration’s February repeal of the 2009 Endangerment Finding, which had provided the scientific foundation for federal greenhouse gas regulations under the Clean Air Act. The administration simultaneously eliminated federal greenhouse gas emissions standards for cars and trucks, according to Reuters.

“The implications for the energy industry are massive,” Orr told the DCNF. “Repealing these rules was absolutely necessary to keep existing coal plants online, and perhaps more importantly, to facilitate the massive buildout of new natural gas power plants needed to meet the nation’s surging demand for electricity.”

That growing data center electricity demand has substantially changed the outlook for natural gas generation since the Biden-era rules were finalized in 2024, pointing to forecasts for significantly higher data center power consumption, Orr said.

“If Republicans maintain control of Congress, they should pass a bill that makes it clear that regulating emissions of greenhouse gases is a federal issue for Congress alone to address and that neither EPA nor the states can regulate emissions on their own,” Milloy said.
